title: Wide-column stores with Cassandra
goal: By the end you can read a CQL primary key as a sorted partition on disk, say what an insert, an update and a delete each leave in the SSTables, spot a tombstone storm before it happens, and choose between a query table, an SAI index, ALLOW FILTERING and a lightweight transaction.

warmup.q: A payout worker inserts each payout into one Cassandra partition per merchant and deletes the row once the payout is paid. Today 50,000 payouts came and went for M-0042, and 10 are waiting. What does reading the next 10 cost?
options: About 10 rows: deleted rows are gone, so the partition holds 10
About 50,010 entries: every delete left a tombstone the read has to step over
Nothing extra after a few minutes, because compaction removes deleted rows right away
It depends only on the LIMIT, because Cassandra stops after 10 rows
warmup.why: A Cassandra delete writes a tombstone, and compaction may drop it only after `gc_grace_seconds`, 10 days by default, so other replicas can't bring the row back. A read from the front of the partition steps over every tombstone before it finds 10 live rows. Past 100,000 tombstones in one read, Cassandra aborts the read. The LIMIT counts live rows, not what the node had to read to find them.

sections.h: A table is a map of partitions, and each partition is a sorted list of rows
sections.body:
Lesson 2 gave the payment history its own Cassandra table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE payments_by_account (
    account_id   text,
    created_at   timestamp,
    payment_id   text,
    merchant_id  text,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    currency     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC);
```

The inner parentheses hold the partition key; the columns after it are clustering columns. This lesson opens the box: what that key means on one node, what a write leaves on disk, and why deleting rows can make reads slow.

Start from the question the table answers: A-1001's 20 newest payments, out of 50 million. A store keyed by payment id would have them scattered over every node, as lesson 2's first version did. So Cassandra groups rows. Every row with the same partition key belongs to one partition. The coordinator hashes the partition key to a token, a 64-bit number (A-1001's is -4994511478997274402), and the token picks the replicas, as in lesson 5. Each replica holds the whole partition, so a query that names the partition key talks only to those nodes.

Inside the partition, the rows are kept sorted by the clustering columns: newest `created_at` first, with `payment_id` breaking ties. Nothing sorts them at read time. The order is how they sit in memory and on disk. "The 20 newest" means "the first 20 rows of one partition", and a time window is one contiguous slice: the node seeks to the first row inside the window and reads until it leaves it. Oldest first is the same slice, read from the other end.

That shape gives the family its name. A partition is Bigtable's row from lesson 1, and the clustering values play the part of its sorted column names, so a partition is a "wide" row that can hold many entries. It never splits across nodes, which is why the Cassandra docs advise keeping one under 100,000 rows and 100 MB. An account that takes millions of payments over the years needs a time bucket in its partition key, such as `((account_id, month), created_at, payment_id)`.

The query rules follow from the picture. The partition key needs `=` on every column, or there's no token and no node to ask. Clustering columns can be restricted only from the left, because that's the only order the rows are in, with at most one range at the end. Anything else means reading rows and throwing most of them away, and CQL refuses unless you add `ALLOW FILTERING` (section 4). So you build one table per query, and the service writes each payment to every table that needs it.

**A partition is a sorted list of rows that Cassandra never edits in place: every write, updates and deletes included, adds a new timestamped piece, and every read merges the pieces it finds.** The stepper shows the sorted list. Sections 2 and 3 add the pieces.

try.title: Watch a write land in its sorted place
steps: From the `labs` folder, start Cassandra 5.0: `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait` (about one to two minutes). Load lesson 2's tables: `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-02-payments.cql`.
Open a prompt with `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh` and run the four statements below. Before the third, predict which rows come back and in which order.
Leave Cassandra running: the next three Try-its use it.

code.title: in cqlsh
code.src:
-- 1. A-1001's partition: one token, rows stored newest first
SELECT token(account_id), account_id, created_at, payment_id
FROM payments.payments_by_account WHERE account_id = 'A-1001';

-- 2. a new payment from 09:00, written last
INSERT INTO payments.payments_by_account
    (account_id, created_at, payment_id, merchant_id, status, amount_minor, currency)
VALUES ('A-1001', '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000', 'pay-81723', 'M-0042', 'AUTHORIZED', 2500, 'EUR');

-- 3. a time window: one slice of one partition
SELECT created_at, payment_id, status FROM payments.payments_by_account
WHERE account_id = 'A-1001'
  AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 08:00:00+0000' AND created_at < '2026-11-07 10:00:00+0000';

-- 4. the same slice, oldest first
SELECT created_at, payment_id, status FROM payments.payments_by_account
WHERE account_id = 'A-1001'

sections.h: Every write is an append: commit log, memtable, SSTable
sections.body:
A payment changes state several times: AUTHORIZED, then CAPTURED, then SETTLED. An Oracle `UPDATE` finds the block that holds the row and changes it in place, keeping the old value in undo for readers who still need it. The block has to be in memory first, which often means a random read before the write. Cassandra, which Facebook first built for its inbox search, takes the other road: a write never reads anything first, and a file is never changed once it's written.

The write path is the LSM tree from the database internals track (LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters, dbi-05) in one line: the node appends the write to its commit log so it survives a crash, adds it to the memtable, a sorted structure in memory, and acknowledges. When the memtable is full, the node flushes it to disk as an SSTable, an immutable sorted file. Nothing is looked up first. Three things follow, and each one surprises people who come from SQL.

First, `INSERT` and `UPDATE` are the same operation, an upsert. An `UPDATE` of a row that doesn't exist creates it. An `INSERT` of a primary key that already exists overwrites the columns it names, with no duplicate-key error. "Insert only if absent" needs a lightweight transaction (section 4).

Second, every cell carries its own write timestamp, in microseconds. The Java driver 4.19 stamps each statement with the application server's clock (its default, `AtomicTimestampGenerator`) unless the statement says `USING TIMESTAMP`. When a read finds two versions of a cell, the higher timestamp wins: lesson 6's last write wins, column by column. An `UPDATE` of `status` writes only the status cell, so after two flushes the row exists as two pieces in two SSTables, and every read stitches them together. The Try-it dumps both pieces.

Third, a read may have to look in the memtable and in several SSTables. Bloom filters let it skip SSTables that can't hold the partition, and compaction keeps the count of SSTables down: in the background it merges several into one new file, keeps the newest version of each cell and drops the rest. Which files it merges is the compaction strategy. Size-tiered (STCS) merges files of similar size, and it's still the default in the `cassandra.yaml` of 5.0.9. Leveled (LCS) arranges files in levels so a read touches fewer of them, at the price of rewriting data more often. Time-window (TWCS) groups data by write time, which suits rows that all expire after the same TTL. Cassandra 5.0 added the Unified Compaction Strategy (UCS), which can be tuned to behave like any of the three; its docs recommend it "for most workloads", and the `cassandra_latest.yaml` that ships with 5.0 makes it the default. For a new table on 5.0, start with UCS.

sections.h: A delete is a write too: tombstones, TTL and the tombstone storm
sections.body:
Delete a test payment, pay-81655, from A-1001's history. Its three replicas are A, B and C, and C is down for an hour. The first version of a delete removes the row from A and B. Then C comes back, and read repair or anti-entropy repair (lesson 6) compares the copies: C has a row that A and B don't have. Nothing tells repair whether A and B lost the row or deleted it, so it copies the row back. The deleted payment returns.

So Cassandra makes a delete a write. It writes a tombstone, a marker with a timestamp that says "this row was deleted at t". The tombstone takes the same write path to every replica and beats older versions by the same timestamp rule. Repair now has something to spread, and C gets the tombstone too.

How long must a tombstone stay? Until every replica has it. Cassandra can't know when that is, so it keeps each tombstone for `gc_grace_seconds`, 864,000 seconds (10 days) by default, and only after that lets compaction drop it. That's the deadline from lesson 6: repair every node more often than every 10 days. A node that stays down longer, then rejoins and is repaired, still has the old row, and the tombstone that should shadow it is gone everywhere else. Repair copies the row back, and the delete is undone. Operators call those rows zombies.

A TTL works the same way. `INSERT ... USING TTL 86400` gives the cells an expiry 24 hours out, which suits idempotency keys. After that the cells are dead: reads skip them and count them as tombstones, and compaction drops them once `gc_grace_seconds` have passed.

Now the failure. A payout worker uses a table as a queue: one partition per merchant, one row per payout, sorted by payout id, and the worker deletes each row once the payout is paid. Every delete leaves a tombstone at the front of the partition, and the tombstones stay for 10 days. When the worker asks for the next 10 payouts, the read starts at the front and steps over every tombstone before it finds 10 live rows. After 1,990 paid payouts, it handles 2,000 entries to return 10. With more than 1,000 tombstones in one read Cassandra logs a warning (`tombstone_warn_threshold`), and with more than 100,000 it aborts the read (`tombstone_failure_threshold`). That's a tombstone storm, and the Try-it starts one.

There are two fixes. Start the slice after the tombstones: keep the last paid payout id and ask for `payout_id > ?`, so the node seeks past them, as the figure shows. On the same partition with 1,200 tombstones, that read reports "Read 3 live rows and 0 tombstone cells". Or don't delete at all: put a time bucket in the partition key and let old buckets expire with a TTL, on TWCS, which drops whole expired files. A real work queue belongs in Kafka, where reading a message doesn't delete anything.

sections.h: Off the key: ALLOW FILTERING, SAI indexes and lightweight transactions
sections.body:
Sooner or later someone needs a query the tables weren't built for. Support wants every FAILED payment from today. The CQL error from lesson 2 offers `ALLOW FILTERING`, and it's tempting, because on a laptop it works. The Try-it's trace shows what it does: "Submitting range requests on 17 ranges", then "Executing seq scan across 1 sstables", then "Read 7 live rows". The node walked every token range and read every row of every partition to return two. With 50 million payments on 12 nodes, each request reads 50 million rows on 12 nodes. `ALLOW FILTERING` is fine in one case: when the query also names the partition key, so the cost is one partition, which you've already kept small.

The second option is a new table, `failed_payments_by_day`, written next to the others. For anything on a hot path that's still the answer.

The third, new in Cassandra 5.0, is a storage-attached index (SAI): `CREATE INDEX ... USING 'sai'`. Each node indexes only its own data, and the index files are built and compacted along with the memtable and SSTables they describe. A query on `status` alone now reads only matching rows, but it still asks every node, because any node may hold a FAILED payment: the trace still says 17 ranges. So SAI is right for a query that runs a few times a minute, or to filter inside one partition (`account_id = ? AND status = ?`). It's wrong for the authorization path, and every write pays to keep it up to date.

The last tool fixes something the write path made impossible. AP4 says an idempotency key may be used once. Two retries of the same payment reach two coordinators at the same moment. Both `INSERT` the key, both succeed because an insert is an upsert, the later timestamp wins, and both requests believe they created the payment. `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` turns the insert into a lightweight transaction (LWT): the replicas first agree, through a round of the Paxos consensus protocol, that the row is absent, and only then write. The reply has an `[applied]` column, and when it's `False` it carries the row that won. The CQL docs warn that LWTs "incur a non-negligible performance cost": a Paxos round adds several round trips between replicas to the write. Use them for the few writes that must not race, like claiming a key. Lesson 10 shows how Paxos makes this safe, and what Cassandra 6 adds for transactions across partitions.

This lesson treated the cluster as one box that stores partitions. Lesson 13 opens the box: how a key finds its replicas on the token ring, how snitches place copies across racks and datacenters, how gossip tells every node who is alive, and how a coordinator runs a read or a write. Lesson 14 sets a cluster up from `cassandra.yaml`, adds and removes nodes, and keeps it healthy with `nodetool`.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra: CQL data manipulation (ALLOW FILTERING, IF NOT EXISTS, USING TTL)
Apache Cassandra 5.0 features: Storage Attached Indexes (project blog)

analogy: Think of a filing drawer for each account, where every payment slip is filed in date order. Nobody ever erases a slip. To change a payment you file a newer slip for it, stamped with the time; to delete one you file a red "void" slip. A reader pulls the slips for a date range and keeps the latest stamp for each payment. Once in a while a clerk recopies the drawer, keeping only the latest slip per payment (compaction), but keeps the void slips for ten days, because two other offices hold copies of the drawer and haven't all seen them yet. A drawer used as an inbox fills with void slips that every reader has to flip past. The analogy breaks on the stamps: a clerk would notice two slips stamped a second apart from two different offices, while Cassandra trusts whichever clock reads later, even a clock that is wrong.
in_your_world: In Oracle, a payment's status lives in one row that each `UPDATE` changes in place. In Cassandra each status change is a new cell with the application server's timestamp, so the clocks on your Quarkus pods matter: keep NTP healthy, or a pod running 2 seconds fast wins arguments it shouldn't. A Kafka consumer that writes payments into Cassandra gets idempotency almost free, because replaying a message writes the same key with the same values. Deletes are where teams get hurt: a table used as a work queue for a settlement batch, or "clean up the processed rows" jobs, fill partitions with tombstones that every read pays for. Put the queue in Kafka, bucket tables by time, and claim idempotency keys with `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS USING TTL 86400`, so a Temporal activity that retries finds the key already taken.
mistake: The most common mistake is using a Cassandra table as a queue, or any insert-then-delete pattern on one partition: pending payouts, jobs, outbox rows. It looks harmless, because the table has the right key and deletes return instantly. People expect a delete to remove data, as it does in SQL. Instead every delete adds a tombstone that stays for at least 10 days, and every read that starts at the front of the partition steps over all of them, until reads slow down and then fail at 100,000 tombstones. The fix: keep queues in Kafka; in Cassandra, bucket partitions by time and let old buckets expire with a TTL instead of deleting rows, and read from a saved position (`payout_id > ?`) so slices start after the dead rows.

compare.title: One status change: Oracle edits a row, Cassandra adds a piece

a.label: Oracle: update in place
a.title: SQL*Plus

b.label: Cassandra: append and merge
b.title: sstabledump of two SSTables
b.src:
UPDATE payments.payments_by_account SET status = 'CAPTURED' WHERE ...;

== nb-1-big-Data.db  (the original insert, unchanged)
'2026-11-07T09:00:00.000Z', 'pay-81723' | [amount_minor=2500 ts=1794081362991451], ...,
                                          [status=AUTHORIZED ts=1794081362991451]
== nb-2-big-Data.db  (the update: one cell)
'2026-11-07T09:00:00.000Z', 'pay-81723' | [status=CAPTURED ts=1794081383953194]

-- a read merges both pieces; compaction later writes one merged row

compare.note: Oracle keeps one current version of a row in one place, and an update has to find it first. Cassandra never finds anything before a write: it adds the new cell with its timestamp, and the old one stays on disk until compaction merges the files. That's why Cassandra writes are cheap and steady under load, and why reads may touch several files. It's also why there's no "row not found" or "duplicate key" on a plain write, and why a delete has to be a marker rather than an erase.

worked.title: Redesign the payout queue so reads never wade through tombstones

steps.say: Write the access patterns first. The worker asks for the oldest waiting payouts of one merchant; support looks a payout up by id. About 30,000 payouts a day for a busy merchant.
steps.code:
P1  next waiting payouts of a merchant, oldest first   ~every second
P2  one payout by id                                    ~a few per minute
volume: 30,000 payouts a day for M-0042

steps.say: The first draft is a queue: one partition per merchant, delete each row once it's paid. Count what a read meets after one day: tombstones live 10 days, so they pile up.
steps.code:
PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id), payout_id)       -- delete when paid

after 1 day:   ~30,000 tombstones at the front of M-0042's partition
after 4 days:  ~120,000 -> past tombstone_failure_threshold: P1 fails

steps.say: Stop deleting. Bucket by hour, so a partition only ever holds one hour of payouts, and record the state as a column. Let whole buckets expire after a week with a TTL, on TWCS, which drops expired files whole.
steps.code:
CREATE TABLE payouts_by_merchant_hour (
    merchant_id  text,
    hour         timestamp,
    payout_id    timeuuid,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, hour), payout_id)
) WITH default_time_to_live = 604800
  AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
                    'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS', 'compaction_window_size': 1};

steps.say: The worker keeps its position: the hour bucket and the last payout it handled. Each read starts after that point, so it never reads old rows at all. Marking a payout paid is an update of one cell, not a delete.
P2 gets its own small table, written with the payout. It expires with the same TTL, so nothing is ever deleted by hand.

lab.title: Build one Cassandra table: sorted partitions, SSTables, tombstones and compaction
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. All twelve fail with `NotImplementedError`.

Read `WideColumnTable.kt`. `insert`, `delete`, `flush` and `repairFrom` are given: writes only ever add a `Version` to the memtable, and `flush` turns the memtable into an immutable `SSTable`. Each `Version` is a whole row with one timestamp; real Cassandra keeps one per cell.
Write `filteringReason`, following rules 1 to 5 in its KDoc. The messages are Cassandra's own, from lesson 2's Try-it.

Write `mergedPartition`: for each clustering key, the newest version across the SSTables and the memtable. Then `select`: refuse, pick partitions, walk the merged rows, count live rows and tombstones, stop at the limit. Ten tests pass now, including the tombstone storm.

Write `compact`. The last test is lesson 6's warning made real: purge a tombstone after `gc_grace`, repair from a replica that missed the delete, and the row comes back. Change `gcGrace` in the test to 60 and watch the first half of that test fail, then put it back.
hints: Rule 1 is one line: `if (!q.where.keys.containsAll(key.partitionKey)) return ALLOW_FILTERING`.
For rule 3, the restricted columns are `q.where.keys + listOfNotNull(q.range?.column)`. A clustering column at index `i >= fixed` that's restricted is a gap, unless `i == fixed` and it's the range.

In `mergedPartition`, the sources are `sstables.mapNotNull { it.partitions[partition] } + listOfNotNull(memtable[partition])`. Use `newer(version, old)` to decide, never `>` on timestamps yourself: it handles the tie, where the tombstone wins.
In `select`, skip rows outside the slice with the given `inSlice` only when `filteringReason(q)` is null. A filtering query reads every row of the partition, and that cost is the point of the test.
In `compact`, `v.deadSince(now)` is null for a live row. Drop a row when `deadSince + gcGraceSeconds <= now`.

drill.title: Claim a key once, and follow a delete to the end
drill.prompt: From memory, write the CQL table for AP4 (an idempotency key and the payment it created), the statement that claims a key exactly once and expires after 24 hours, and what the reply looks like when the key is taken. Then list, in order, what happens to a row from `DELETE` until it's gone from disk.

answer.src:
CREATE TABLE payments.idempotency_keys (
    idem_key   text PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id text
);

INSERT INTO payments.idempotency_keys (idem_key, payment_id)
VALUES ('idem-7f3a', 'pay-81723')
IF NOT EXISTS USING TTL 86400;

--  [applied] | idem_key  | payment_id      when the key is taken:
--      False | idem-7f3a |  pay-81723      the reply carries the winner

-- a DELETE, from start to end:
-- 1. a tombstone with the delete's timestamp goes to the commit log and memtable of each replica
-- 2. reads see it shadow every older version of the row, and count it as a tombstone
-- 3. flushes and compactions carry it along for gc_grace_seconds (864000 s, 10 days)
-- 4. repair spreads it to any replica that missed it, inside those 10 days
-- 5. after that, the next compaction of its files drops the tombstone and the row together

recap: A Cassandra table is a map of partitions. The partition key is hashed to a token that picks the replicas; inside a partition, rows are stored sorted by the clustering columns, so a range read is one slice.

Writes never edit in place: commit log, memtable, then an immutable SSTable. `INSERT` and `UPDATE` are both upserts, every cell carries a write timestamp (client-side in the Java driver), and reads merge pieces from several SSTables, newest timestamp wins.
Compaction merges SSTables and drops superseded cells. STCS is the 5.0.9 `cassandra.yaml` default; UCS, new in 5.0, is recommended for most workloads and is the default in `cassandra_latest.yaml`.
A delete or an expired TTL is a tombstone, kept for `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days) so repair can spread it. Repair more often than that, or deleted rows come back as zombies.

Insert-then-delete on one partition causes tombstone storms: a warning past 1,000 tombstones in a read, failure past 100,000. Use Kafka for queues, time buckets with TTLs, and slices that start after the dead rows.

Off the key: `ALLOW FILTERING` scans every partition (fine only inside one partition), an SAI index still asks every node, and `IF NOT EXISTS` is a Paxos-backed lightweight transaction for the few writes that must not race.

quiz.q: Table `payments_by_account` has `PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)` with `created_at DESC`. Which query reads one contiguous slice of one partition?
options: `WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07' AND created_at < '2026-11-08'`
`WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-07' ALLOW FILTERING`
`WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND payment_id = 'pay-81723'`
`WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' ORDER BY amount_minor DESC`
quiz.why: It gives the partition key with `=` and one range on the first clustering column, so the node seeks to the window and reads until it leaves it. Without the account there's no token. `payment_id` alone skips `created_at`, so it's a gap Cassandra refuses without `ALLOW FILTERING`. And `ORDER BY` works only on clustering columns, in stored or reversed order.

quiz.q: Two services set the status of pay-81723 one second apart, the first to CAPTURED, the second to VOIDED, both with plain `UPDATE`s through the Java driver. The second service's pod clock is 3 seconds slow. What does a read return afterwards?
options: VOIDED: Cassandra applies writes in the order they arrive
An error, because two updates touched the same cell
CAPTURED: each cell keeps the highest timestamp, and the driver stamped the second update with the slow clock
Both values, as siblings for the application to merge
quiz.why: The Java driver 4.x stamps each statement with the client's clock by default. The VOIDED write carries a timestamp 2 seconds older than CAPTURED, so last write wins keeps CAPTURED on every replica, and the void disappears without an error. Cassandra has no siblings; that's Dynamo with vector clocks, in lesson 9.

quiz.q: Why does Cassandra write a tombstone for a delete instead of removing the row from each replica?
options: Because removing data from an SSTable would need a full rewrite of the file
So that a replica that missed the delete can't have the row copied back to the others by repair
So that the delete can be undone within `gc_grace_seconds`
Because tombstones make reads faster than missing rows
quiz.why: If the replicas that saw the delete simply forgot the row, repair would find it on the replica that was down and spread it back. The tombstone is newer than the row, so it wins the merge and repair spreads the delete instead. Immutable SSTables are true too, but a delete could still be a removal in the next compaction; the distributed copies are the reason, as the Cassandra docs say. Tombstones can't be undone, and they make reads slower.

quiz.q: Support wants every FAILED payment of the day, a few times an hour, and the team adds `CREATE INDEX ... ON payments_by_account (status) USING 'sai'`. What does a query on `status` alone now do?
options: Reads one partition, because the index stores the partition of every FAILED payment in one place
Asks every node, and each node reads only its matching rows through its own index
The same full scan as `ALLOW FILTERING`, because SAI only works with a partition key
It's refused: an indexed column still needs `ALLOW FILTERING`
quiz.why: SAI is a local index: each node indexes its own SSTables and memtables. A query without a partition key can't know which nodes hold FAILED payments, so it visits every token range (17 in the Try-it), but each node reads only matching rows instead of all of them. That's fine a few times an hour and wrong on a hot path, where a query table wins.

quiz.q: From lesson 6: a node was down for 12 days, longer than `gc_grace_seconds`, while a payment was deleted on the other two replicas. It comes back and `nodetool repair` runs. What happens to the payment?
options: It stays deleted: repair always prefers the majority
It stays deleted, because hinted handoff delivers the tombstone
Repair fails with an error until the node is rebuilt
It can come back: compaction may have purged the tombstone on the other two, so repair copies the old row back to them
quiz.why: Repair compares Merkle trees and copies whatever is newer or missing. Once the tombstone is gone from the other replicas, the stale node's row is the only version left, so it wins. Hints don't help: the default `max_hint_window` is 3 hours, and repair doesn't vote by majority. That's why every node must be repaired more often than `gc_grace_seconds`.

flashcards.front: What do the partition key and the clustering columns each decide?
flashcards.back: The partition key is hashed to a token: which replicas and which partition. The clustering columns decide the sorted order of rows inside the partition.

flashcards.front: What happens on a Cassandra write, in order?
flashcards.back: Append to the commit log, add to the memtable, acknowledge. Later the memtable is flushed to an immutable SSTable. Nothing is read first.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between INSERT and UPDATE in Cassandra?
flashcards.back: Almost none: both are upserts that write cells with a timestamp. There's no duplicate-key error and no "row not found".

flashcards.front: Who sets a cell's write timestamp when you use the Java driver 4.x?
flashcards.back: The client: the default `AtomicTimestampGenerator` uses the application server's clock, unless the statement says `USING TIMESTAMP`.
How long compaction must keep a tombstone before it may drop it: 864,000 s, 10 days. Repair every node more often than that.
`tombstone_warn_threshold: 1000` logs a warning; `tombstone_failure_threshold: 100000` aborts the read.
When the query also gives the full partition key, so the filter runs over one small partition. Without it, every partition on every node is read.

terms.plain: All rows with the same partition key, stored together and sorted by the clustering columns, on each of the key's replicas.
The primary-key columns after the partition key; they set the order of rows inside a partition.
A node's in-memory, sorted table of recent writes, flushed to an SSTable when full.
A write that inserts the row if it's absent and overwrites the named columns if it's present. Every Cassandra INSERT and UPDATE.
A timestamped marker that a row or cell was deleted or has expired; kept for gc_grace_seconds so repair can spread it.
The rule for which SSTables a node merges: size-tiered, leveled, time-window, or unified (UCS, 5.0).
Cassandra 5.0's secondary index: each node indexes its own data alongside its memtables and SSTables.
A conditional write (`IF NOT EXISTS`, `IF col = ?`) that runs a Paxos round among the replicas before applying.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Deletes in Cassandra are free, they return in a millisecond. Let's keep pending payouts in a table and delete each one when it's paid." Explain what a delete really writes, why it has to, and what this design does to the worker's reads after a few days.
explain_back.answer: A delete in Cassandra doesn't remove anything. It writes a tombstone, a marker with a timestamp, through the normal write path, which is why it's fast. It has to be a write because the data lives on three replicas: if the replicas that saw the delete just forgot the row, repair would find it on a replica that was down and copy it back. The tombstone is newer than the row, so it wins the merge and repair spreads it instead. Cassandra keeps tombstones for gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default, before compaction may drop them. In a queue partition, every paid payout leaves a tombstone at the front, and the worker's "next 10" read starts at the front, so it steps over all of them. At 30,000 payouts a day, the read meets 30,000 tombstones after one day, logs warnings past 1,000, and fails outright past 100,000, after about four days. I'd keep the queue in Kafka, or bucket the table by hour with a TTL and have the worker read from its last position, so no read ever starts in the dead rows.

deeper.body:
Cassandra 5.0 also ships newer storage formats that its default `cassandra.yaml` leaves off. The `cassandra_latest.yaml` in the same 5.0.9 image turns them on: trie-based memtables (`TrieMemtable`), the BTI SSTable format (`sstable: selected_format: bti`, a trie-indexed format that replaces the old partition index and summary files) and UCS as the default compaction. The default file sets `storage_compatibility_mode: CASSANDRA_4`, so a cluster upgraded from 4.x keeps writing files 4.x could read; that's why the Try-it's files are named `nb-...-big-...`. A new cluster can start from `cassandra_latest.yaml` instead.

Two tools from the Try-its are worth keeping. `sstablepartitions`, new in 5.0, lists the largest partitions in an SSTable, which is how you find the account that broke the 100 MB guideline before it hurts. `sstablemetadata` prints, among other things, an estimate of droppable tombstones per file.

Materialized views were Cassandra's attempt to maintain lesson 2's "one table per query" for you: you declare a view with a different primary key and the server writes it. The Cassandra docs still mark them experimental, and most teams write the extra tables from the application, often in a logged batch. A logged batch guarantees that if any statement in it is applied, all of them eventually are, which is what you want when one payment goes to three tables. It isn't isolated: a reader can see one table updated before the other.

ScyllaDB speaks CQL and runs the same data model on a C++ engine, so this lesson's tables and queries work there unchanged. Since its 2025.1 release it's source-available rather than open source.
